extracted.intended_audience: military legal officers, judge advocates, commanding officers who convene or review courts-martial
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretive guidance on the Articles of War governing jurisdiction, statute of limitations, trial procedure, approval/review of sentences, mitigation/pardon powers, records, and courts of inquiry for military trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of charge particulars (Art. 62)
rubrics_metrics.description: A charge alleging assault with a rifle and infliction of a mortal wound upon a fellow soldier, with particulars of time and place clearly stated, sufficiently alleges an offense within the sixty-second article of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: specifying time and place in the specification will sustain a trial under Art. 62; particulars must be clear enough to allege the offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on second trial for same enlistment misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A subsequent trial under the same enlistment for another discovered misrepresentation or concealment would be a second trial for the same offense within the meaning of the article prohibiting double jeopardy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited holdings indicate that charging again for the same core offense arising from the same enlistment can constitute double jeopardy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsideration by reconvened court-martial not a new trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconsideration by a court-martial of a finding, whether guilty or not guilty, when duly reconvened for that purpose, is not a second trial; original and revised proceedings are parts of the same trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a court is duly reconvened to reconsider its own finding, that proceeding is treated as a continuation, not a new prosecution (authorities cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court of inquiry opinions not equivalent to adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: An opinion given by a court of inquiry is not in the nature of a sentence or adjudication pronounced upon a trial; it cannot be pleaded as a former trial, acquittal, or conviction in a subsequent court-martial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court of inquiry is investigative/ advisory; its opinions do not constitute prior adjudications for double jeopardy pleas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promptly vest military jurisdiction where duty-related defense possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a soldier on duty (e.g., sentinel) commits an act that may be excused as performance of military duty, charges should be immediately formulated and lodged to vest military jurisdiction before civil courts assume jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: to secure military forum and preserve military-case issues, file charges and secure vesting of jurisdiction at once (cited G.O. 21694).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and finality of general courts-martial under Art. 62
rubrics_metrics.description: General courts-martial may take cognizance, under the sixty-second article, of all crimes not capital committed by an officer or soldier within the territory where he is serving; although jurisdiction is concurrent with civil courts, if a court-martial first acquires jurisdiction its judgment is entitled to the same finality as a civil court's decision on issues within its jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil courts generally cannot disregard a military conviction merely for error not affecting military court's jurisdiction; jurisdictional defects, however, remain open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double jeopardy contingent on jurisdiction of prior tribunal
rubrics_metrics.description: A person is not put in second jeopardy unless the prior acquittal or conviction was by a court having jurisdiction to try him for the offense charged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For double jeopardy protection to attach, the prior tribunal must have had lawful jurisdiction over the accused and offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military acquittal bars later civil trial in U.S.-created Territory
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier acquitted by a military court-martial of competent jurisdiction for a homicide committed in the Philippine Islands cannot be subsequently tried for the same offense in a civil court exercising authority in that Territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holding emphasizes the territorial/sovereignty context where the territory's authority derives from the U.S.; military judgment is final between the same sovereign authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil assumption of jurisdiction and surrender on demand (sentinel cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil authorities may assume jurisdiction in cases (e.g., sentinel firing causing accidental third-person death) and the military should surrender custody on civil demand; the right of civil authorities to hold the soldier is to be raised by habeas corpus in U.S. courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When civil authorities properly assert jurisdiction, military custody should be surrendered rather than litigating the jurisdictional issue at the post level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post commander's duty when civil warrant issued after summary trial
rubrics_metrics.description: If a soldier has been tried by a summary court and a formal demand is later made for surrender to civil authorities, the post commander should surrender the offender rather than refusing based on prior summary trial; double jeopardy issues are for the civil tribunal to decide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application of the 59th Article: commanding officers should not adjudicate civil jurisdictional warrants on the spot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'order for such trial' (reference of charges)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'order for such trial' within the article's meaning is the reference of the charges to the court for trial, not merely the order appointing the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The operative act creating the trial is referring charges to the court; procedural formalities appointing the court are distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment does not automatically constitute 'impediment' to prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere fact that the offense was concealed by the accused and remained unknown to military authorities for more than two years does not constitute an 'impediment' preventing timely prosecution under the relevant article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alleged concealment/unknown whereabouts without further qualifying facts is insufficient to invoke statutory impediment exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegation of unknown whereabouts is not good averment of manifest impediment
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere allegation in a specification that the whereabouts of the offender were unknown during an interval exceeding two years is not a valid averment of a 'manifest impediment' within the statute's meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleas relying only on absence-of-knowledge averments will be insufficient without stronger factual showing of impediment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on trial after discharge subject to Article 103
rubrics_metrics.description: Liability to trial after discharge (or after expiration of enlistment term) is subject to limitations prescribed in Article 103; the limitation is a defense that must be specially pleaded and proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleadings: limitation is an affirmative defense requiring special plea and proof; plea of guilty waives the limitation; under not-guilty plea, evidence may show limitation has taken effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'absence' for limitation purposes (fleeing from justice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'absence' referred to (e.g., 'having absented himself') is intended to mean leaving one's home/residence or concealing oneself with intent to avoid detection or punishment—analogous to 'fleeing from justice'—not merely being outside U.S. territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecution need not prove the accused left U.S. territory; absence within jurisdiction suffices if it evidences intent to avoid detection/punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of limitations for desertion: when rule changed by 1890 amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to the April 11, 1890 amendment, statute of limitations for desertion began to run only upon return of the deserter to military control; after amendment it begins to run at the end of the term for which the soldier was enlisted or mustered into service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use enlistment/muster term as the trigger post-amendment; cited cases clarify application (C. 4130 etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: No limitations running for desertion in time of war
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute of limitations does not run in cases of desertion during time of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What constitutes 'time of war' may be based on existence of warlike conditions and operations even without formal declaration (see further rubric about definition of time of war).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'time of war' for limitations (warlike conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'in time of peace and not in the face of an enemy' is interpreted to mean the statute runs where the U.S. is confronted with warlike conditions and has an enemy; conversely, when forces are confronting strikers, rioters, or engaged in active operations (e.g., Indian outbreaks), those conditions may be treated as 'time of war' for limitations purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis is factual—presence of warlike conditions/active operations controls whether limitation applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing rules for multiple desertions and effect of making good time
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a soldier deserts, is convicted, given a sentence less than dishonorable discharge, later deserts again, or deserts and later makes good time lost, the statute of limitations for the later desertion begins to run at times determined by whether the soldier returned to control, the end of enlistment, or when he finished making good time per Article 48 and relevant holdings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple scenarios are governed by case law (G. 15257, etc.); calculating the limitation requires detailed timeline of convictions, returns to duty, and time-made-good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence from U.S. means absence from U.S. jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Article 103, 'absence from the United States' means absence from the jurisdiction of the United States; temporary presence on a government vessel under the same name may not constitute such absence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical import: service overseas on government transport under one's known identity generally will not be treated as statutory absence; authorities cited (C. 21760, 28321).

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 103 applies to escape (escape not continuing offense)
rubrics_metrics.description: The one hundred and third article applies to escape; escape is not considered a continuing offense for purposes of the statute of limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Escape is treated as a discrete offense subject to the article's timing rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation start for fraudulent enlistment (pay/allowances rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases of fraudulent enlistment (except where enlistment occurred without a discharge from prior enlistment), the limitation provided in Article 103 begins to run from the date the accused received last pay or allowances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Last pay/allowances is the operative date for the limitations period in fraudulent-enlistment cases (C. 13322).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal character required for approval of sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Approval of a sentence must be of a formal character; an indorsement of a single word 'approved' may be irregular/objectionable though sometimes sufficient in law; mere forwarding of records without an approval notation is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approval must explicitly indicate approval of the sentence (not only findings). Cases hold mere recommendation or forwarding is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approval by convening/ordering officer shows non-disapproval
rubrics_metrics.description: Approval required by the officer ordering the court (where that officer in fact approves) serves to show that he has not disapproved and is the proper compliance with the article even if he lacks authority to give full effect to certain sentences (e.g., dismissal in peace).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An approving endorsement by the convening officer is the expected act; it demonstrates that the reviewing chain did not disapprove.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewing authority when units transfer commands
rubrics_metrics.description: If men tried by a general court-martial pass with their command from the department in which tried before action by the reviewing authority, the commanding general of the department in which they were tried is the proper reviewing authority for the cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where unit movement precedes review, determine reviewing authority by where the trial occurred and who succeeded to that command (cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'officer commanding for the time being'
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'officer commanding for the time being' is an officer who has lawfully succeeded to command of the officer who convened the court (e.g., relieved, merged commands); such successor is authorized to act upon the record as reviewing authority and should indicate on proceedings that he succeeded to the command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successor need not be of the rank originally required to convene courts; lawful succession, not rank, is the test (C. 10849 et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Successor need not meet original convening rank requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary that the 'officer commanding for the time being' be of the rank required of a convening officer; he need only have lawfully succeeded to the command to act upon a record of trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical: do not invalidate review solely for successor's rank so long as succession to command was lawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mergers/discontinuance of commands and proper reviewing officer
rubrics_metrics.description: When a command (division/brigade/post) is discontinued or merged into a larger command before review, the commander of the larger/receiving command (division, corps, department) is the proper 'officer commanding for the time being' and thus the reviewing officer who may act on the proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court convened by now-nonexistent subordinate commands need not be dissolved; successor commanders assume review duties (multiple cited rulings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Illness/disability of commander and acting reviewing authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Illness of a department commander constitutes a 'disability' under which the senior line officer present and on duty in the department is the 'officer commanding for the time being' for review purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporary incapacity transfers review authority to the senior on-duty line officer until the commander resumes duty or is replaced legally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department commander authority to confirm dismissal in war
rubrics_metrics.description: A department commander may confirm a sentence of dismissal of an officer and order its execution while a state of war continues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: War condition expands confirming authority in certain cases (C. 5860, 6240, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: President as confirming authority for certain commands
rubrics_metrics.description: When a division or separate brigade does not belong to a separate army in the field, the President of the United States is the proper confirming authority under the one hundred and seventh article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-level confirming authority applies to specified organizational contexts; consult the article for exact scope (G. 4980, 10910).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewing authority should formally approve before forwarding to President
rubrics_metrics.description: A reviewing authority should first formally approve the sentence; forwarding the record without such approval is incomplete and irregular, though the President may subsequently act under a different article if needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal recorded action by reviewing authority clarifies the procedural posture of the record and proper chain for presidential action.

rubrics_metrics.name: President's power to approve/disapprove and remit/mitigate
rubrics_metrics.description: The President, upon receiving a record, may approve or disapprove the sentence in whole or in part and may exercise the usual power of remission or mitigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The President's clemency and mitigation powers are broad and include remission and mitigation subject to procedural rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardoning/remission power not delegable by military commander
rubrics_metrics.description: A military commander vested with power of pardon or mitigation under the article may not delegate that power to an inferior officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegation attempts (e.g., department commander authorizing post commander to remit) are invalid; only the designated commander may exercise the power (authorities cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewing officer other than President cannot commute punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: A reviewing officer other than the President is not empowered to commute a punishment; the 'pardon' specified for reviewing officers is remission and does not include commutation or conditional pardon; thus they cannot commute a dishonorable discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigation by reviewers is limited to reducing quantity/quality within same species; commutation (changing species) is beyond their authority (R. 48 etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Only President can remit/commute death or dismissal sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Power to remit or commute sentences of death (and dismissal in case of an officer) remains with the President; departmental action attempting commutation of death sentence is null but may be treated as a recommendation to the President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any commutation of capital sentences must come from the President; subordinate action has no legal effect except as recommendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewing officer cannot change the kind/species of punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: The order prescribing maximum punishments does not authorize the reviewing officer to change the kind (species) of punishment; substitution powers vested in the court do not vest in reviewing officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: reviewer substituting confinement for forfeiture would be an illegal mitigation if it changes the species of punishment (cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardoning power may be exercised as long as material for exercise remains
rubrics_metrics.description: The pardoning power under the article is not limited to the moment of approval of the sentence but may be employed as long as there remains any material for its exercise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clemency applications may be considered at later stages if materials remain that permit exercise of pardoning authority (multiple R. and C. authorities cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of transfer to penitentiary on clemency jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: A military prisoner sentenced to confinement in a penitentiary or the U.S. military prison is, for clemency purposes, considered to have passed beyond the jurisdiction of a division or department commander from the date of approval of his sentence (regardless of temporary retention pending transfer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application: clemency petitions in such cases are forwarded to The Adjutant General for Secretary/President action per regulation; reviewing authority may mitigate to military prison where legal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewing authority's mitigation powers (reduce quantity/quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reviewing authority, if he deems the punishment too severe, may graduate it to the proper measure by reducing it in quantity or quality without changing its species (mitigation). Imprisonment, fine, forfeiture of pay, and suspension are punishments capable of mitigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: three-year penitentiary sentence mitigable to two years in military prison; reviewer may reduce term or severity but not alter punishment type into another species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illegal punishment not capable of validation by mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: A punishment that is illegal in itself is not capable of mitigation; attempting to mitigate an illegal imprisonment to confinement in another place does not cure illegality—both remain invalid and inoperative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the original punishment was unauthorized, mitigation cannot make it lawful; legal basis for punishment must exist before mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonorable discharge not mitigable except by President
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence of dishonorable discharge by a court-martial cannot be commuted or mitigated by reviewing authority except by the President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only presidential intervention can change the nature of dishonorable discharge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigation power follows transferee commander when prisoner station changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the station of a soldier undergoing a sentence imposed by an inferior court is changed, the power to mitigate the sentence passes to the new post commander.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority to act on mitigation is tied to current station command; transferring a prisoner transfers mitigation jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to copy of court-martial record (Art. 114)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the one hundred and fourteenth article and War Department practice, every person tried by a general court-martial or military commission is entitled to one copy of the record of proceedings upon demand made by him (or by a representative) before his death; application should first be addressed to the Judge Advocate General; others may obtain copies only by Secretary of War order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant is not the accused, must exhibit satisfactory evidence of representation; Judge Advocate General's report is not furnished under this article.

rubrics_metrics.name: No obligation to order court of inquiry on officer's application
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither the President nor a commanding officer is obliged to order a court of inquiry on the application of an officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts of inquiry are discretionary and may be refused; cited cases show denials are upheld.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court of inquiry not proper for patent-infringement opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: A court of inquiry should not be convened for the purpose of obtaining an opinion on patent infringement; such a request is not a proper subject for a court of inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts of inquiry are for military rights, responsibilities, conduct—not for civil/commercial legal opinions like patent infringement (C. 25188).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and procedure of courts of inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: A court of inquiry can examine into transactions of officers or enlisted men only; the accused may appear and examine witnesses as freely as before a court-martial; proceedings may be open at the court's discretion; courts of inquiry rarely opine on pure legal questions and should confine opinions to whether further court-martial proceedings are called for or to special military questions proposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts of inquiry are investigatory boards, not trials; their opinions should address military issues and whether trial is warranted; procedural norms include open hearings at discretion and generally allow challenges in interest of justice.
